title: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery
summary: Cloud Infrastructure Discovery is the enumeration step an adversary performs after obtaining credentials for an infrastructure-as-a-service environment, and it is broad by design. The target is everything the credential can see: compute instances, virtual machines, snapshots, volumes, storage buckets, and managed databases. Providers expose this through documented control plane interfaces, so the activity consists of read-only API calls or CLI commands rather than anything inherently malicious. The adversary uses a compromised access key to establish the effective permission set, mapping what exists, what is exposed, and what the identity is allowed to change, which shapes later decisions about persistence, staging, or exfiltration. Cloud audit logs record every one of these calls with the caller identity, source address, user agent, and parameters, so this phase is one of the most reliably observable even though each individual call is legitimate. Detection depends on volume and shape rather than on any single event: bursts of listing calls across many services in a short window, enumeration from a new address or an unusual user agent, sequencing that resembles a script rather than a human console session, and read calls against security configurations such as public access block settings that operational roles rarely query. Unlike cloud service discovery, the focus here is the components inside the services, not the service catalogue itself.

beginner.definition: Cloud infrastructure means the virtual machines, disks, copies and storage buckets inside a cloud account. This technique is an attacker listing all of those things. They use stolen access keys to ask the cloud provider what exists. The provider answers honestly, because the request uses real credentials.
beginner.whyItMatters: Before attackers act, they want to know what is there and what they can reach. Listing everything shows them the valuable data and the weak spots. Each request is a normal, allowed action, so it is hard to block. However, the requests are recorded, so the pattern can be spotted. Missing this step means you may not notice an intrusion until data has already gone.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains cloud access keys, often from a stolen file or a weak role.
They call interface commands that describe machines, disks and snapshots.
They list storage buckets and check which ones are publicly readable.
They query databases to learn sizes, owners and network rules.
They repeat this across services to build a map of the account.
The results guide their next choice, such as where to hide or what to copy.
beginner.example: Think of a new caretaker in a large building. Before starting work they walk every corridor and open every door just to see what is inside. They take nothing. A trained guard would still notice someone testing every handle in the building in one afternoon.
takeaways: Read-only cloud calls still leave useful records in activity logs.
Look for wide, fast listing across many services by one identity.
Remove unused access keys and grant only the permissions needed.

objectives: Define cloud infrastructure and the resources an attacker enumerates.
Explain how read-only interface calls reveal an attacker reconnaissance.
Recognise enumeration patterns such as broad listing in a short period.
Use cloud activity logs to attribute discovery to an identity and address.
Distinguish this technique from cloud service discovery.
